claim: For every integer \(r\ge2\), let \(X=\mathbb P(1^r,a,b)\) with \(1\le a\le b\). Among the canonical members, the singular locus is zero-dimensional (possibly empty) for exactly \(3\Phi(r)\) weight pairs, where \(\Phi(r)=\sum_{m=1}^r\varphi(m)\); among the terminal members the corresponding count is \(3\Phi(r-1)\). Hence exactly \(3\varphi(r)\) canonical non-terminal boundary pairs have zero-dimensional singular locus. They are precisely \(b-a=r\) with \(\gcd(a,r)=1\), or \(a=r+(b-a)\) with \(1\le b-a<r\) and \(\gcd(b-a,r)=1\). Consequently the proportion of zero-dimensional-singular-locus spaces in either the canonical or terminal family tends to \(6/\pi^2\).

correctness.rationale: The singular-locus criterion follows from stabilizers of the weighted C* quotient: positive-dimensional singular locus occurs exactly when gcd(a,b)>1. The symbolic canonical/terminal triangles then reduce the census to coprime lattice points, giving 3 Phi(r), 3 Phi(r-1), and boundary difference 3 phi(r). The independent brute-force regression through r=400 matches all formulas and the explicit boundary description.
